en: The Ritual for Cultivating and Realizing the Vows of Samantabhadra from the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, Compiled by the Song Dynasty Jinshui Śramaṇa Jingyuan. Chapter One:
General Exposition of the Origins Chapter Two: Adorning and Purifying the Site of Practice (*Mārgakṣetra*)
III. The Method for Purifying the Body; IV. Invocation of the Sages and Holy Ones;
V. Contemplative Practice and Offering; VI. Praising the Tathāgata; VII.
Paying Homage to the Triple Gem; VIII. Cultivating the Five Repentances.
Circumambulation and Recitation; The Ninth: The Ritual for Chanting Sutras; The Tenth:
A General Account of the Origins. First:

In the past, regarding the *Commentary on the "Aspiration for Enlightenment"* (*Pranidhāna*) by Qingliang [Zongmi], it expanded upon the wondrous source and exhausted its profound depths and distant reaches through nothing but meditative concentration and wisdom.

The Patriarch clearly elucidated the provisional and the ultimate, extracting the profound from the obscure and the subtle from the minute. He composed the *Yi-chao* (Commentary on the Meaning) to expand upon it;
thus, all those throughout the world who drive their discourse [on the teachings] have attained the underlying intent by following his words.

As for the meticulous investigation of the profundities of the nine assemblies and the collation of the treasures of the ten practices, these are preserved in the *Yuánjué Chàn-yí* (Ritual for the Repentance of Perfect Enlightenment), wherein the regulations and models are fully provided.
Jingyuan: I have long been concerned that those who transmit the teachings and contemplations of our patriarchs in recent times instead practice the liturgical texts of other schools.
How is this different from having a virtuous ancestor yet remaining ignorant of it? This is something even a gentleman would find shameful.
In the winter of the second year of the Xining era, while revising the *Complete Enlightenment Repentance Ritual*, I was thus able to purify my brush and wash away [delusions].
This "Yan" (Inquiry) is a collection of refined texts, sought from like-minded companions for study and cultivation.
Since its foundation rests upon a profound basis, I have employed the titles of the scriptures as chapter headings and inscribed them at the beginning.

This is intended to ensure that future readers may investigate the grand efficacy of wisdom and concentration and revitalize the flourishing virtue of the "Qingliang" (Cool and Refreshing) school. Thus, these words shall further provide succor and be transmitted to infinity.

(The nine assemblies and ten practices are all contained within the extensive ritual text for repentance. From this point onward, the nine sections follow the *Complete Enlightenment Repentance* [Yuánjué Chàn], differing only slightly in their expansion and contraction.)
Purifying the Site of Enlightenment, Part Two:
Now, one who wishes to invoke the sages and worthies must also purify the altar site. If it is not clean, the mind for the Way will not arise, and there will be nothing to move their descent.
Therefore, one should adorn the altar, make offerings to the Triple Gem, and seek compassion through repentance of transgressions.
Regarding all evil karma within the world, the method for the *dāna* site (*dānasthāna*) requires that one first select a location free from clamor, impurity, evil, and various obstacles.
If one finds a deep mountain ravine or a secluded forest spring, it is most excellent.
If it is in a human habitation, one must remove one or two feet of old soil and smear the ground with fragrant mud. Then, hang...
Among the various banners and flowers, place an image of Vairocana in the center. On either side, place images of Mañjuśrī and Samantabhadra.
Before the Buddha, install a copy of the *Samantabhadra-caryā-praṇidhāna-sūtra* contained within a casket.

If you have the capacity, consult the sūtra and its commentaries to create a circular mandala painting depicting the seven locations and nine assemblies, and hang it around the perimeter. Light lotus lamps and burn a hundred [incense sticks].
Regarding incense and various ornaments, they need only be pure; they need not be exceedingly expensive.

Each should offer them for worship to the sages and worthies according to their own means, solely to manifest one's own devotion. How could the sages and worthies have preferences for the good or the bad?
As for the method of arranging them, it may be done as one pleases; there is no fixed ritual. This applies to the initial practice of the preparatory methods, and...

As for their formal cultivation, it is always performed on the six days of the fast (ṣaḍ-upoṣadha). On these days, the messengers of the Four Heavenly Kings and various celestial benevolent deities descend to the human realm to inspect good and evil.

Upon seeing those who practice cultivation, they offer comfort and protection, manifesting auspicious signs so that those who behold them will give rise to joy in their hearts and have their faculties enhanced.
Section Three: Methods for Purifying the Body.

Now, clothing and the physical form are both the bases upon which the practitioner’s mind relies. If one wishes to cultivate this Great Practice of the Perfect and Sudden Teaching, one must first perform prostrations and repentance (*li-ch'an*).
Regarding the method of prostrations and repentance, it is essential that the mind be pure. For the mind does not arise in isolation.
One must rely upon conditions; when the conditions are pure, the mind is likewise pure. Therefore, one must strictly purify one’s clothing and physical form.

Now, those who have left the household life ought by nature to maintain purity. If, during ordinary times, one fails to observe this with diligence, then upon entering the *dōjō*, one must don fresh, clean garments.
If no new ones are available, one must wash and launder old ones. Next, one must bathe.

One bathes the body. If the body is defiled by contact with impurities, how can it be fit to approach the sages and worthies? Although the Buddhas harbor no aversion toward such persons, the deities will not provide protection.
When the deities do not provide protection, malevolent spirits and demons will cause affliction and confusion, giving rise to obstacles and hindrances.

It is not merely that the body must be purified; one must likewise purify the mind. One must sever all discursive thoughts and devote oneself single-mindedly, recollecting the Dharma being practiced throughout the day.

During the six periods of the night, one should pay homage to and invoke the Triple Gem. One must not make excuses for negligence or succumb to sleep, nor should one harbor thoughts of worldly affairs for even a single moment.

One should maintain vigilant guard so that [unwholesome states] do not sprout; when the three karmas are thus disciplined, even if one encounters obstructive conditions, there shall be no regression or loss.
The Fourth Section: Petitioning the Sages and Worthies.
(When the practitioner first enters the ritual arena, they should recite the name of Samantabhadra Bodhisattva, circumambulate it once, and proceed to the front of the Dharma seat.)

Having spread out the *niṣīdana* mat, one should stand upright with the body straight and the palms joined. One should first cultivate thoughts of loving-kindness toward all sentient beings, vowing to rescue and deliver them.
Next, transcending ordinary states of mind, one should reverently invoke the Triple Gem. Although the Buddhas and the worthy sages are omnipresent, [one should nevertheless call upon them].
If one does not reverently invoke [the Buddha], he will stand before one yet remain unmanifest. Therefore, a sutra says: "For example, when the sun rises, it appears universally throughout the world;
its reflection appears in every vessel of pure water. The Buddha-sun is likewise: it appears universally throughout the dharma-realm without before or after.
Within the mind-vessels of all sentient beings that are pure, there is no one before whom the Buddha does not appear. Now, you should maintain single-minded right mindfulness and be cautious.
Do not be distracted. Prostrate with the five limbs touching the ground and pay homage to all the Three Jewels. (The one who leads the chant [shengde zhe] calls out:
"All with reverence" (from here on, the assembly chants together):
"With single-minded devotion, we prostrate to the eternally abiding Three Jewels throughout the ten directions and the entire Dharma-realm."

(Perform one prostration as a general salutation to the Triple Gem. Having completed the kneeling position (*hukuei*), hold the incense burner and burn various famous incenses to reverently invite the sages and worthies.

However, perform this invitation only once; it need not be done on other occasions. Nevertheless, in the liturgical manuals of various families, offerings of incense and flowers always precede the ritual.)
Now, according to the ritual of the Perfect Enlightenment Sūtra (in all cases, one first makes this invocation):
With single-minded devotion, I reverently invoke: Homage to the Buddha Vairocana, the Original Honored One, whose ten bodies are first perfected;
who, when his perfect awakening was first achieved, did not depart from Jambudvīpa but ascended to the heavens; and who manifests infinite clouds of bodies. (Bow once for each invocation.)

With single-minded devotion, we take refuge in and entreat: the Buddha Amitābha, who universally gathers all lands of defilement; the King of Great Vows, who has received the prediction of enlightenment from all Buddhas throughout the Flower Adornment Sūtra;
and all Buddhas of the ten directions and three periods of time within the Flower Treasury World-system, who have now come together into this assembly.

With single-minded devotion, we take refuge in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra of the Buddha’s Great Vaipulya*. It rends asunder the profound and subtle mysteries; it is the distinct teaching of the One Vehicle.
Its vast and boundless expanse comprises all twelve divisions of the sūtras.

With single-minded devotion, we offer this invocation: Homage to the Lord of the Avataṃsaka Sūtra, who does not abandon the gateway of causes, who illuminates the practices and vows, and who universally encompasses all that is profound and wondrous—Mahāsattva Samantabhadra Bodhisattva (The Master of Repentance at the Site of Enlightenment; three invocations and three prostrations).
With single-minded devotion, we take refuge in and entreat the Buddhas of the seven locations and nine assemblies, who manifest as sovereigns and their retinues:
Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva, Bhadramukha Bodhisattva, and all the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas as numerous as atoms found within the various chapters.
With single-minded devotion, we pay homage to the fifty-five true spiritual friends who are the leaders of the final assembly in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*.
Having sought the Dharma through a hundred cities, they perfected their realization in a single lifetime—namely, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas such as Sudhana and the rest.
With single-minded devotion, we take refuge in and entreat: Namu Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva; Mahāsthāmaprāpta Bodhisattva; Maitreya Bodhisattva;
Aśvaghoṣa, Nāgārjuna, and all the patriarch bodhisattvas; and all the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas of the ten directions and the three periods of time.
With single-minded devotion, we pay homage: To Śāriputra and the six thousand bhikṣus of the final assembly;

to all the noble Saṃgha of Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas—both those still in training and those beyond training—who dwell throughout the realm of empty space and within every atom of all buddha-fields.
With single-minded devotion, we offer this invocation: Homage to those within the assembly of the *Avataṃsaka* who constantly make great vows to bring peace to humanity and protect the Dharma;
to Brahmā, Śakra, and the Four Heavenly Kings; to the eight classes of beings, including devas and nāgas; to the Vajrapāṇi deities; to the deity who presides over space;

and even to all the deities who preside over various worlds, as well as those within this kingdom who govern the virtuous and punish the wicked, the deities who protect the monastery, and those who maintain the Right Dharma.
Regarding the Dharma: all worthy ones and sages (this section merely requests that one should not prostrate; for laypeople, there is no hindrance).

This is the fifth [section] on the practice of contemplative offerings (the eightfold sequence consisting of: offering, praising, reverent salutation, repentance, requesting [the turning of the wheel], sympathetic joy, dedication, and making vows).
This is the fundamental practice of a practitioner, not some separate method. The World-Honored One cited it in full within the *Sūtra of the Questions of the Bodhisattva Vimalamati*.
It is also an essential gateway for entering the *Avataṃsaka*. Therefore, after the sūtra has extensively explained the wondrous functions of the merits of all Buddhas, it subsequently states:
"If one wishes to accomplish this gateway of merit, one should cultivate ten kinds [of practices]."
The vast practices and vows have been extracted from the sūtras by the masters of the Way in the Western Regions (India) and circulated separately for recitation and cultivation.
There have been three translations: first, by Buddhabhadra of the Jin dynasty; second, by the Tripiṭaka Master Amoghavajra of the Tang dynasty;
and third, by the commentator on the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* and others during the Zhenguan era. These ten practices and vows are precisely this offering.
These are the eight [sections]. However, within the section on "Exhortation" (*adhyeṣaṇā*), two gates are further distinguished: "Turning the Wheel of Dharma" and "Remaining Long in the World.
Furthermore, within the section on "Dedication" (*pariṇāmanā*), two gates are differentiated: "Following the Buddha's Example" and "Accordance with Sentient Beings. Thus, they constitute ten phrases.

Having completed the exhortation to the Triple Gem, may their compassion respond to my invocation and come to meet my karmic conditions. Looking up in reverence to all Buddhas and all holy sages, like clouds...
The assembly gathers at the site of enlightenment, filling the entirety of space. Knowing and seeing us, we entreat you with a sincere and earnest heart.
We should offer worship with incense and flowers. The Holder of the Incense Burner (Shengde) shall hold the burner and chant:
All these assemblies knelt before one another and, reverently holding incense and flowers, made offerings according to the Dharma.
(At this point, cease chanting. With hands joined in reverence, hold up the flowers and should give rise to contemplative practice, visualizing according to the Sūtra as follows:

Within every single atom of all Buddha-lands throughout the entire Dharma-realm and space-realm, across the ten directions and the three periods of time—within each and every one of these atoms, there are...
In all worlds, before as many Buddhas as there are atoms in a minute particle, each surrounded by an ocean-like assembly of various Bodhisattvas,
I— by the power of my vows of universal aspiration— arouse deep faith and understanding, perceiving them directly before me,
and offer to them all manner of supreme and exquisite offerings. These are so-called clouds of flowers, clouds of garlands, clouds of celestial music, and clouds of heavenly...
Clouds of parasols; clouds of celestial garments; clouds of various celestial incenses—unguents, burning incense, and powdered incense—each as vast in measure as Sumeru, the King of Mountains;
various lamps being lit, such as lamps of ghee and lamps of oil, each lamp-wick as large as Mount Sumeru and each lamp-oil as vast as the waters of the great ocean—with all such offerings.
[End of] the equipment. Constantly making offerings, one visualizes and then scatters flowers, chanting:
"May these clouds of fragrant flowers fill the realms of the ten directions; within lands as numerous as atoms, may they be offered to all Buddhas."

May the Honored Dharma, the Bodhisattvas, and the assemblies of Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas all become clouds of exquisite flowers, incense, and various offering implements, constantly performing offerings.
May the Triple Gem universally accept these clouds of incense and flowers, taking them as luminous pedestals.
Extensively throughout boundless realms, performing boundless buddha-works. (Chant "Raising [the hands] and standing," while the Sound-Virtue Master says:
Having completed the offerings, all pay homage with reverence. (Together, perform one prostration.)
(Consulting the *Sūtra on the Three Oceans of Contemplating the Buddha*, it states that within the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), one should offer flowers of grass and wood.

That practitioners today mostly offer flowers made of silk and brocade is likely because it is the season of frost and snow. At other times, one should seek to follow that sūtra in making respectful offerings to the Triple Gem.)
Praising the Tathāgata, Part Six:

Having made these offerings, one should immediately straighten one’s body and demeanor, stand attentively with a single mind, and join in praising the subtle and wondrous merits of all Buddhas and Samantabhadra.
Therefore, after citing as many Buddhas as there are atoms in a dust mote, the Sūtra continues: "I shall, with all..."
They possess profound faith and understanding. Manifesting before them, their wisdom and insight each surpass those of the goddess Sarasvatī.

From their subtle organ of the tongue, they produce oceans of inexhaustible sounds; from each and every sound, they produce oceans of all forms of speech, extolling and praising the oceans of merit of all Tathāgatas.
"Profound faith" refers to the power of contemplative wisdom (*vipaśyanā-jñāna*). This is one's own...
The cause is likewise the power of Samantabhadra’s Dharma as the condition. Thus the Sūtra says:
"Because the realm of empty space, and even the afflictions, have no end, my praise has no exhaustion. This applies to all ten types of practice and vow, which collectively are thus.
One should know that it is necessary to contemplate so that one's practice becomes clear; only then will both the praiser and the praised be vast, profound, and inexhaustible.
The light of wisdom is like the pure sun; Replete with all practices, it is like the full moon.
Its merit is ever-filling, comparable to the great ocean; Stainless and unimpeded, it is like space.
All lands throughout the ten directions Are entirely purified and adorned in a single kṣaṇa.
Turning the wheel of Dharma with wondrous sounds, Pervading the world, there is none equal to you;
The body and marks of Samantabhadra are like space, Abiding in reality, not in a land.
According to the desires of the minds of all sentient beings, He manifests his universal body, equal to all.

Universally manifesting boundless vows of merit, Bestowing happiness upon all sentient beings, Relying on practice and vows until the end of the future, Constantly and diligently cultivating the means to deliver all beings.
(After the praise, one should explain the purpose of establishing the repentance ceremony. According to one’s own...)
Wisdom and Power: I request that you set forth this clearly; do not resort to evasive speech). Section Seven:

Reverence for the Triple Gem (Having completed the praise, one should also give rise to contemplative practice. According to the sutras, one should visualize as follows: "Throughout the entire Dharma-realm and the realm of empty space...")

To all the Buddhas, World-Honored Ones, as numerous as the atoms in all Buddha-fields throughout the ten directions and the three periods of time, I, by the power of the practices and vows of Samantabhadra, believe and understand with a profound mind as if they were standing before my very eyes; with all the pure actions of body, speech, and mind, I [make offerings].
I constantly practice prostration and reverence. At the site of each and every Buddha, I constantly manifest bodies as numerous as the atoms within unspeakably, unspeakably many Buddha-fields.
With each body, I universally prostrate before Buddhas as numerous as the atoms within unspeakably, unspeakably many Buddha-fields.
Even if the realm of empty space were to come to an end, my prostrations would not cease; for since the realm of empty space is inexhaustible, these prostrations of mine are likewise inexhaustible.
With reverence that is inexhaustible, even unto the exhaustion of the karma of body, speech, and mind, I prostrate with single-minded devotion.
At the moment the ten bodies first reached fulfillment and you attained perfect enlightenment, you did not depart from Jambudvīpa, yet ascended to the heavens.
To the inexhaustible clouds of bodies, the Honored One Vairocana Buddha, I pay homage with single-minded devotion.
Universally gathering the defiled lands, he cultivates great practices and vows; born through transformation from lotus flowers, all receive their prophecy.

Homage with single-minded devotion to Amitābha Buddha. As he utters words of praise and enters meditative concentration, all Buddhas bearing the same name as Dharmamati— such as Guṇakānanā and others— manifest before him.

With single-minded devotion, I pay homage. Light radiates from between his eyebrows, exhorting those on the ten stages. Together with the Buddhas of the ten directions, he shares the eloquence of the Dharma-gate of Vajragarbha.
With single-minded devotion, I pay homage. Within the "Chapter on Manifestation," his great practices are praised; all proclaim this Dharma, and they are all named Samantabhadra.

With single-minded devotion, I prostrate before as many Buddhas as there are atoms; all the Buddhas of the ten directions and the three periods of time throughout the atom-like lands within the Flower Treasury World described in the entirety of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*.
With single-minded devotion, I pay homage to the Avataṃsaka Sūtra of the Buddha, the Great Vaipulya. It cleaves open the profound and subtle mysteries;
the distinct teaching of the One Vehicle is vast and complete, encompassing all twelve divisions of the scriptures.

With single-minded devotion, prostrate. To the Lord of the Assembly at the Fruit of Buddhahood within the Bodhimaṇḍa, who has elucidated the Ten Vows and universally encompassed all that is profound and wondrous—the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Samantabhadra (the Master of the Practice and Vows; here, one should perform three prostrations).
With single-minded devotion, I pay homage to the Ten Leaders of the Assembly on the Ten Faiths, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas, in the Hall of Universal Radiance.
With single-minded devotion, I pay homage to the Ten Wisdom Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas, the Leaders of the Assembly on the Ten Abidings, in the Palace of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.
With single-minded devotion, I pay homage to the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Daśavanas, Lord of the Assembly of the Ten Practices, in the Yāma Heaven Palace.
With single-minded devotion, I pay homage to the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Daśaketus, Lord of the Assembly of the Ten Dedications, in the Tuṣita Heaven Palace.
With single-minded devotion, I pay homage to the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Vajragarbha, Lord of the Assembly on the Tenth Stage in the Palace of the Heaven of Making Use of Others' Transformations.

With single-minded devotion, I pay homage to him who, in the Reunion at the Hall of Universal Radiance, has manifested the arising of the Tathāgata-nature, wherein the cause is perfected and the fruit is fulfilled.
I single-mindedly prostrate to the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Wondrous Virtue (Guna-ratna),
who, at the Universal Radiance Hall during the third assembly, revealed and developed the practice of progressive cultivation. I also prostrate to the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Good Wisdom (Sudhi).
With single-minded devotion, I pay homage before the Tathāgata in the Jeta Grove, who has realized the Dharmadhātu,
to the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Mañjuśrī.

With single-minded devotion, I pay homage to the leaders of the final assembly, the fifty-five true spiritual friends, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas of provisional and ultimate truth. With single-minded devotion,
I pay homage to those of perfect faculties and superior vessels, the models for cultivation and realization, who sought the Dharma through a hundred cities and perfected it within a single lifetime.
The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Sudhana prostrates with single-minded devotion before Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva, Mahāsthāmaprāpta Bodhisattva, Maitreya Bodhisattva,
and the ancestral Bodhisattvas such as Aśvaghoṣa and Nāgārjuna, who have manifested their traces in pure lands, as well as all Bodhisattvas of the ten directions and the three periods of time.

Mahāsattva, with single-minded devotion, prostrate yourself. At the conclusion of this assembly, there are Śāriputra and six thousand bhikṣus, as well as all the śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and noble saṅgha—
both those still in training and those beyond training— who reside within the realm of empty space and throughout every atom of all buddha-fields.
The Eighth: Cultivating the Five Repentances.

(Regarding these five, first we clarify repentance (*pratikramana*). As for offenses, there are those of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-āpatti*) and those of prohibition (*pratiṣedha-āpatti*); as for repentance, there are the phenomenal and the principial.

Phenomenal repentance, as found in sutras such as the *Vaipulya-buddhanāma-sūtra*, encompasses all ten thousand practices and must involve earnest supplication and prostration before the Buddhas of the ten directions.)

The Buddha [instructs]: "Lay bare the characteristics of your transgressions and reproach yourself with profound remorse. Perform the ritual confession as described in the *Vimalakīrti Sūtra*: contemplate that the nature of sin is empty, existing neither internally nor externally;

simply by generating the bodhicitta, the afflictions as numerous as the sands of the Ganges will naturally be eliminated. Only after clarifying both principle (*li*) and phenomena (*shi*) should one benefit others.
Then, practice the remaining four types of repentance. (End of quote).
First, the Method for Repentance:

Having finished prostrating to the Buddha, straighten your body and maintain a dignified demeanor; with reverent devotion, kneel on the ground with the right knee touching the earth and burn various famous incenses.
Visualize the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra, adorned with immeasurable ornaments and surrounded by his retinue, acting as the presiding master of the confession, as if standing directly before you.
With single-minded focus and profound shame and remorse, reveal all evil karma created throughout immeasurable kalpas.
Once these karmic obstructions are removed, pure precepts and virtues are accomplished; therefore, while the sutra text universally refers to this as "confessing karma," in reality—
Regarding the three obstacles and the four obstacles, there are none that one does not repent of. One should contemplate with single-minded focus, saying:

"For myself and all sentient beings, regarding all karmic obstacles of sin committed since beginningless time, I pray only that the Triple Gem will take pity and deliver us. May our ignorant karma be instantly dispelled and transformed into pure causes.

May body and mind together become empty, and may both sin and merit be found to have no master. May we clearly perceive the true nature and become equal to the Dharma-body of the Buddhas. [The sins of] the three karmas...

[The sins] are cleared away. The three liberations are accomplished, and the heavy obstructions of the six sense organs are transformed into the six supernatural powers. Having thus visualized, one proclaims aloud with a clear voice:
"For the sake of the four debts of gratitude, the three realms of existence, and all sentient beings of the Dharma realm, I vow to sever and eliminate all obstacles. I take refuge and repent."
(Having finished chanting, rise and prostrate. One should then cultivate the ten minds of reversal and compliance. Silently contemplate the *Qīngliáng gē* [Verses on Coolness] as follows:

"Since beginningless time, ignorance has arisen; likewise, evil friends have increased my afflictions. Without a mind of sympathetic joy, all goodness is forever extinguished, while evils of body, speech, and mind gradually grow.
Thought after thought, they pervade everywhere and defile every contact; moment after moment, they continue in succession, busying themselves day and night. I do not desire..."
People who know how to conceal their faults do not fear the evil realms, acting with reckless abandon. Lacking both shame and remorse, they are caught in the net of Māra;
denying cause and effect, they fall into the pit of icchantikas. Having thus followed the current and turned their backs on the source, the ocean of birth and death has overflowed in vast expanse.

Fortunately, you, son of a noble family, recognize its origin and now wish to go against the current, abandoning the poor village. With right faith in cause and effect, you shatter the icchantika views.
Cultivating shame and remorse breaks the lack of conscience among humans and devas; fearing the evil realms breaks fearlessness; confessing sinful karma breaks concealment;
severing discursive thoughts and continuing the flow of the mind breaks constant attachment; generating the bodhicitta breaks pervasive arising;

cultivating merit to compensate for faults breaks self-indulgence; guarding the true Dharma breaks joylessness; mindfulness of the Buddhas of the ten directions breaks association with evil friends; and contemplating the nature of sin [breaks ignorance].

The six preceding verses on "Emptiness Destroying the Fetters" take the ten minds that accord with birth and death as their objects of treatment in the first three [verses], and the ten minds that oppose birth and death in the latter three [verses], overturning and destroying them from the end backward.
One should recite these silently and contemplate them thoroughly, then speak these words:
I, Bhikṣu [Name], with a sincere heart, repent. I, together with all sentient beings of the Dharma-realm, should reflect upon myself:
throughout the beginningless kalpas of the past, driven by greed, hatred, and delusion, I have committed immeasurable and boundless evil karmas through body, speech, and mind.
If these evil karmas possessed any substantial form or characteristics, even the entirety of the realm of empty space could not contain them.

I now, with my three karmas entirely purified, universally before all the Buddhas and the assemblies of Bodhisattvas throughout the Dharma-realm and within every atom-sized world-system, sincerely repent.
Hereafter, I shall not create [evil] again, but shall constantly abide in pure precepts.

Regarding all merits, I now further reflect that, blinded by ignorance, I have committed endless transgressions, obstructing the causes of the Buddha-dharma and opening the gate to the icchantika state.
On the road, they contravene the holy intent and follow after evil conditions; they abandon bodhicitta and indulge in the cycle of birth and death.

Regarding the Dharma of renunciation, they lack even a single thought of aspiration. Having long accumulated the causes of various bitter poisons through habitual practice, they defile those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), as well as kin and non-kin alike.
Toward renunciants, they revile, scold, and rebuke them; they associate with those of evil dharma and defile stupas and monasteries, violating their vows of purity.

Regarding the precepts: our bodies and minds have been dissolute; we have envied those who are virtuous and have acted with hostility toward our teachers and elders. Possessing both craving and delusion, we lack both shame and remorse.

We reflect upon our own meager merits, which have brought us birth among the ranks of humanity. Fortunately, we have encountered the final age of Śākyamuni’s teaching and have left the household life to study the Way.

Yet, we have not yet been able to illuminate the profound essence of the teachings and contemplations for the sake of self-benefit and the benefit of others. Although we engage in the study of doctrine and provide lectures—

By practicing the categories of the teachings while grasping at signs, one deviates from the fundamental tenets; by contravening the scriptures and turning one's back on reason, one praises oneself and slanders others, thereby wasting the offerings of the faithful in vain.

One’s liberation and moral discipline will constantly suffer many lapses and transgressions—whether they be the four grave offenses (*pārājika*), the *sthūlātyaya* offenses, or even all other heavy and light karmic obstructions—one shall surely sink into the miserable realms. I pray that the Triple Gem, the Honored One Vairocana, and [your] vows and practices...

May the Lord of Repentance, Samantabhadra Bodhisattva, take pity and protect me with mindfulness; may he love my repentance, transform the mind of the three poisons into the three secret treasuries, and universally enable all sentient beings to ascend together to the realm of truth.
(Rising, the one who recites the *Śrīguṇa-rāja-sūtra* says:
Having finished the repentance, I take refuge and pay homage to Samantabhadra Bodhisattva and all the Triple Gem (bowing together once).
II. Explaining the Method of Exhortation and Entreaty (From this point onward, the practices of Vow and Conduct are based on the verses of the *Pratideśanā-sūtra*.

Formerly, Master Ciyun Zhiyi, in compiling the *Ritual for Rebirth in the Pure Land*, also adopted various verses from this sutra as the prescribed method. However, through compassionate exhortation and entreaty, one removes the obstacles of slandering the Dharma.)
The roots of goodness of benevolence and compassion arise. While the Śrāvakas seek only their own liberation and merely perform repentance, the Bodhisattvas take pity on the multitudes;
they must therefore exhort all Buddhas to let the rain fall universally, so that both themselves and others may be thoroughly moistened.
I, the bhikṣu [Name], with a sincere heart, make this earnest entreaty:
To all those lamps of the world throughout the ten directions, Who first attained perfect awakening—
I now entreat them all To turn the unsurpassed, wondrous wheel of Dharma.
If the Buddhas wish to manifest parinirvāṇa, I shall entreat them all with utmost sincerity:
"I pray that you remain for as many eons as there are motes of dust in a buddha-field, for the benefit and happiness of all sentient beings.
Having made this entreaty, I take refuge in and pay homage to Samantabhadra Bodhisattva and all the Triple Gem.
The Dharma of Rejoicing in the Threefold Knowledge (The sutra text describes rejoicing in four types of merit. Because one previously did not rejoice in the goodness of others,
one now rejoices in order to celebrate their joy, thereby removing the obstacle of envy and giving rise to impartial virtue).
I, the bhikṣu [Name], rejoice with a sincere heart.
I rejoice in all the merits of all sentient beings throughout the ten directions, of those in the two vehicles—
both those still training and those beyond training— and of all Tathāgatas and Bodhisattvas.
Having expressed sympathetic joy, I take refuge in and pay homage to Samantabhadra Bodhisattva and all the Triple Gem.

Regarding the method of dedication (pariṇāmanā) according to the four clarities: the scripture explicitly clarifies that one dedicates [merit] to sentient beings so that they may attain bodhi. This excludes any ulterior motives.
Dedicating my inferior hindrances so as to give rise to vast goodness that pervades the entire dharma-realm (the meaning of which is identical to the limit of reality),
I, Bhikṣu [Name], dedicate with a sincere heart.
All merit from prostrations, praises, and offerings, The request for the Buddhas to remain in the world and turn the wheel of Dharma,
Rejoicing in, repenting of, and all roots of goodness— I dedicate them to sentient beings and the path of the Buddha.
(Having completed this dedication, I take refuge in and pay homage to Samantabhadra Bodhisattva and the Triple Gem.)
The Method for Making Vows According to the Five Sciences (According to the scriptural text, all ten types clarify vast conduct and vows; therefore, by making these vows,
one eliminates obstacles that cause regression, attains the dhāraṇī of all practices, and swiftly achieves the fruit of Buddhahood).
I, the bhikṣu [Name], make this vow with a sincere heart:
May my actions of body, speech, and mind be ever pure, And likewise may all my practices and buddha-fields be so;
Possessing such wisdom as that of Samantabhadra, May I become equal to him in every respect.
Having made this vow, take refuge and pay homage to Samantabhadra Bodhisattva and all the Triple Gem.
Circumambulate while reciting the ninth invocation:
*Namo* to the Buddhas of the Ten Directions.
Homage to the Buddhas of the ten directions!
Homage to the Sangha of the ten directions!
Homage to the Vairocana Buddha, whose ten bodies were first perfected!
Homage to Amitābha Buddha, who has bestowed the prediction of enlightenment upon all;
homage to all Buddhas as numerous as the atoms in the Flower Treasury World;
homage to the Great Vaipulya Buddhāvataṃsaka Sūtra.
Homage to the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra, who illuminates the practice of vows;
homage to the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī, who clearly reveals faith and understanding;
homage to all the great bodhisattvas of the seven locations and nine assemblies.
Homage to all spiritual friends and the Bodhisattva Sudhana;
homage to all Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas of the ten directions.
(Recite the names of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas. Having circumambulated three times, or seven times, complete this.)
Thereafter, recite the sutra. The rules for reciting the sutra are set forth below. Upon finishing the recitation, chant:
"I take refuge in the Buddha; may all sentient beings perpetuate the lineage of the Buddhas and resolve upon the unsurpassed mind."
Taking refuge in the Dharma, may all sentient beings enter deeply into the treasury of the sutras, their wisdom as vast as the ocean.
Taking refuge in the Sangha, may all sentient beings lead and govern the great assembly, free from all hindrances. Homage to the noble multitude.
This is the tenth rule for the recitation of the sutras.
If one practices the repentance ritual for a single session, reciting (or chanting) the ten major precepts of the Brahma-net Sūtra or the *Pranidhāna-gāthā* within the ritual arena,
one should realize that the sound of the recitation is empty in nature and the body is tranquil— like clouds and like shadows— as one lifts and lowers the feet.
The mind has nothing to be attained; it does not dwell upon the characteristics of movement. Illusory forms are entirely empty, which is itself the true *dharmatā*.
Therefore, this body of mine manifests as reflections throughout the ten directions, filling the *dharmadhātu* without exception or partiality. Having finished reciting the sutra:
Upon arriving before the Buddha, one should recite the Three Refuges and exit by circling to the right.

If this is undertaken at the beginning of the new year or prior to the commencement of the sacred retreat, it may last for a period of seven days, or even up to forty-nine days, as one’s capacity permits.

One must establish a separate hall for meditation and contemplation outside the ritual arena; when chanting the scriptural texts, the phrasing and words must be made distinct and clear. As for the speech...
With eloquence perfected, he projects this Dharma-sound throughout the ten directions, making offerings to the Triple Gem and bestowing it universally upon all sentient beings,
causing them all to realize the Vairocana Tathāgata-garbha Samādhi and the Revolving Ocean of the Dharmadhātu.
